given:
An image whose size is supplied as the tuple image_size = (height, width) = (480, 640) — i.e. width 640, height 480 (note the order: legacy passes (h, w), NOT (w, h); file_manager.py:391, :421). h and w are plain Python ints (file_manager.py:207-222). The segment list is empty and segment_manager.class_aliases is empty, because every normal image load calls _reset_state -> SegmentManager.clear() first (main_window.py:2141; segment_manager.py:19-26; invoked from file_navigation_manager.py:186, :279). A sidecar named <base>.txt sits next to the image and contains exactly three lines:
  '3 0.5 0.5 0.25 0.5'
  '2 0.5 0.5 0.1'
  'cat 1.1 0.5 0.2 0.2'
No .npz, _seg.txt, _coco.json, _CM.npz, .xml or _createml.json exists for that image, because '.txt' is the LAST and lowest-fidelity entry of the load chain (file_manager.py:128-136).
when: load_existing_mask walks the chain, finds only <base>.txt, and calls load_bb_txt(path, (480, 640)) (file_manager.py:173-205, :201). load_bb_txt reads all lines, denormalizes them into integer pixel boxes (file_manager.py:412-451), then hands the whole list to _add_box_segments, which assigns class ids, clamps, drops and fills (file_manager.py:453, :381-410).
then:
Exactly one segment is produced.
  Line 1 '3 0.5 0.5 0.25 0.5' -> x1 = round((0.5 - 0.25/2) * 640) = round(240.0) = 240; y1 = round((0.5 - 0.5/2) * 480) = round(120.0) = 120; x2 = round((0.5 + 0.125) * 640) = round(400.0) = 400; y2 = round((0.5 + 0.25) * 480) = round(360.0) = 360 (file_manager.py:446-449). Clamping changes nothing. mask[120:360, 240:400] = true (file_manager.py:400-401): rows 120..359 and columns 240..399, i.e. 240 rows x 160 columns = 38,400 true pixels inside a fresh 480x640 boolean array. The segment record is exactly {mask: <480x640 bool>, type: 'Loaded', vertices: null, class_id: 3} (file_manager.py:403-409).
  Line 2 '2 0.5 0.5 0.1' has 4 tokens, so it is skipped silently, with no error and no class id (file_manager.py:432-434).
  Line 3 'cat 1.1 0.5 0.2 0.2' -> in IEEE-754 doubles 1.1 - 0.2/2 is exactly 1.0, so x1 = round(1.0 * 640) = 640; 1.1 + 0.2/2 is 1.2000000000000002, so x2 = round(768.0000000000001) = 768; y1 = round(0.4 * 480) = 192; y2 = round(0.6 * 480) = 288. Clamping gives x1 = max(0, 640) = 640 and x2 = min(640, 768) = 640 (file_manager.py:395-396), so x2 <= x1 and the box is dropped (file_manager.py:397-398). The y extent was legal; the drop is caused by x alone.
Surviving segments are appended in file order, one per surviving line, with no de-duplication and no merging of overlaps.
and:
The dropped line still leaves a class behind, and this ordering is part of the contract. _build_label_map runs at file_manager.py:392 over the labels of ALL parsed boxes ('3' and 'cat') BEFORE any clamping or dropping at :394-398. Numeric labels claim their ids first ('3' -> 3 via int() at :365-366), then non-numeric labels take the lowest ids not already taken (:370-377). So 'cat' is assigned class id 0 and segment_manager.class_aliases[0] = 'cat' is registered permanently (:377), even though its only box was discarded. That alias table is copied into every later save (save_worker.py:89; save_export_manager.py:424), so a port that filters boxes before assigning ids would produce identical pixels but a different class id for a later 'cat' box and a different alias table on disk.
And the file is all-or-nothing on arithmetic failure: segments are only added at :453, after the whole parse loop, so an exception raised at :446-449 discards every already-parsed box in the file.
parameters:
image_size = (height, width); x pairs with width, y with height (file_manager.py:391, :395-396).
Line splitting: line.strip().split() — Python's whitespace split, which collapses runs of any whitespace (space, tab, \r, \n, \x0b, \x0c, and Unicode spaces such as U+00A0) and yields no empty tokens. A line must have EXACTLY 5 tokens, else skip (:432-434). Blank lines yield 0 tokens and are skipped. A 6th token (e.g. a YOLO prediction confidence) makes the line 6 tokens -> skipped.
Token order: label, cx, cy, bw, bh — all four coordinates normalized to [0,1] by convention but never range-checked.
Coordinate parse: Python float() (:437-440). Its grammar is NOT JavaScript's Number(): it ACCEPTS 'nan', 'inf', 'infinity', '+inf' (all case-insensitive), '.5', '1.', and underscore separators between digits ('1_0.5' -> 10.5, '1e1_0' -> 1e10); it REJECTS '' , '0x10', '0b101', '0o17', '1,5', '5_', '_5', '1__0', '1e'. JS Number() gets '0x10' -> 16, '' -> 0, 'inf' -> NaN, '1_0' -> NaN, all wrong. Implement a Python-float-compatible parser, e.g. match /^[+-]?(?:inf(?:inity)?|nan|(?:\d(?:_?\d)*(?:\.(?:\d(?:_?\d)*)?)?|\.\d(?:_?\d)*)(?:[eE][+-]?\d(?:_?\d)*)?)$/i, strip '_', then Number(). Only a parse FAILURE skips the line; a successful parse to NaN/Infinity does not (see edge cases).
Denormalize, in this exact association (file_manager.py:446-449):
  x1 = pyRound((cx - bw/2) * w);  y1 = pyRound((cy - bh/2) * h)
  x2 = pyRound((cx + bw/2) * w);  y2 = pyRound((cy + bh/2) * h)
Do NOT algebraically refactor (e.g. to cx*w - bw*w/2): the halving and the add/subtract happen in normalized space BEFORE the multiply, and a different association gives a different double and occasionally a different pixel.
Rounding: Python's built-in round() on a float — round-half-to-EVEN applied to the exact IEEE-754 double, returning an exact integer. Math.round (half-up, and half-up toward +Infinity for negatives) is WRONG. Reference port:
  function pyRound(x){ if(!Number.isFinite(x)) throw new RangeError('non-finite coordinate'); const f=Math.floor(x), d=x-f; if(d>0.5) return f+1; if(d<0.5) return f; return f%2===0 ? f : f+1; }
Verified ties: 10.5->10, 11.5->12, 30.5->30, 240.5->240, 511.5->512, 512.5->512, 2.5->2, -0.5->0, -1.5->-2, -2.5->-2. Python returns an arbitrary-precision int, but since the value is immediately clamped into [0,w] / [0,h], a double is safe once non-finite inputs are rejected.
Clamp, asymmetrically (file_manager.py:395-396): x1 = max(0, x1), y1 = max(0, y1), x2 = min(w, x2), y2 = min(h, y2). There is NO upper clamp on x1/y1 and NO lower clamp on x2/y2 — that asymmetry is what makes wholly-out-of-image boxes collapse and be dropped instead of surviving as a 1-px sliver at the edge.
Drop predicate (:397-398): discard the box if x2 <= x1 OR y2 <= y1. Evaluated AFTER clamping.
Fill (:400-401): a fresh (h, w) boolean array per surviving box, with mask[y1:y2, x1:x2] = true — x2 and y2 are EXCLUSIVE, x1 and y1 inclusive; width = x2-x1, height = y2-y1.
Segment record (:403-409): {mask, type: 'Loaded', vertices: null, class_id}. type is the literal string 'Loaded'; vertices is null, so loaded boxes are masks, not editable rectangles.
Class id resolution (_build_label_map, file_manager.py:345-379), per distinct label string, in two passes over the labels of all parsed boxes:
  pass 1, in first-appearance order: (a) if the label equals an existing alias NAME, reuse that alias's id (:362-363); else (b) if Python int() accepts it, the id IS that integer (:365-366); else (c) queue it as unnamed (:368).
  pass 2: taken = existing alias ids UNION ids claimed in pass 1; each unnamed label in queue order takes the lowest non-negative integer not in taken, and is registered as class_aliases[id] = label (:370-377).
  Python int() accepts an optional sign, ASCII or Unicode decimal digits, and '_' between digits; it is arbitrary precision; it REJECTS '3.0', '0x10', '' and any float-looking token.
edgeCases: MOST IMPORTANT, and absent from the card: a coordinate token that float() accepts but that is not finite does NOT skip its line — it aborts the entire file. 'nan', 'inf', '-inf', 'Infinity', '1e309' all parse successfully inside the try at file_manager.py:437-440, but int(round(...)) at :446-449 sits OUTSIDE that try and raises ValueError ('cannot convert float NaN to integer') or OverflowError ('cannot convert float infinity to integer'). The same happens to a finite value whose product overflows, e.g. cx=1e306 with w=640 (1e300*640 = 6.4e302 is fine; 1e306*640 overflows). The exception propagates out of load_bb_txt before _add_box_segments at :453 ever runs, so ZERO segments load from the file — every valid line before and after the bad one is thrown away. load_existing_mask catches it at :202-204, logs, and continues the chain; since '.txt' is the last entry (:135) the chain then ends with nothing loaded.

A read or decode failure is different and cleaner: open(txt_path) at :424 is called with NO encoding, so OSError/UnicodeDecodeError is caught at :426-428, logged, and load_bb_txt RETURNS normally with zero segments (no exception, chain ends at :205). Both paths end in 'nothing loaded', but only the non-finite path raises.

Encoding is platform-dependent: open() at :424 uses locale.getpreferredencoding(False), which is the ANSI code page on Windows (cp1252 on this machine) and usually UTF-8 on Linux/macOS. A UTF-8 file with a BOM therefore decodes on Windows with 'i>?' (U+00EF U+00BB U+00BF) glued to the first token, so '0' becomes a token int() rejects, and that box silently becomes a NEW named class with a garbage alias instead of class 0.

The class token is never validated as numeric. 'dog 0.5 0.5 0.2 0.2' is fully accepted (:436 unpacks it, :438 parses only the 4 coordinates). '3' resolves to class 3 ONLY if no existing alias is literally named '3' — an alias name match wins over the integer interpretation (:362-366). '3.0' fails int() and gets the lowest free id plus a new alias named '3.0'. '-1' is accepted by int() and becomes class_id -1. A 30-digit token becomes a 30-digit class id in Python; a TS port using Number would silently lose precision there.

Class ids and aliases are assigned BEFORE clamping and dropping (:392 runs before :394-398), so a box that is discarded still consumes an id and, if its label is non-numeric, permanently registers class_aliases[id] = label (:377), which is then written into every save (save_worker.py:89, save_export_manager.py:424). In the worked example class_aliases[0] = 'cat' survives although no 'cat' pixel is loaded.

The drop at :397-398 is broader than 'collapses to zero'. It also removes: boxes with negative normalized width or height (bw = -0.2 makes x1 > x2); boxes entirely outside the image on any side (x1 = -100, x2 = -50 clamps to x1 = 0, x2 = -50, so x2 <= x1); and boxes exactly touching an edge from outside, as line 3 of the worked example shows.

Rounding mode is behaviour-visible, not merely a 1-pixel cosmetic difference. On a 1024x1024 image, '0 0.5 0.5 0.0009765625 0.5' gives edges 511.5 and 512.5, so Python yields x1 = 512 and x2 = 512 and the box is DROPPED, while Math.round yields 512 and 513 and the box SURVIVES with width 1. A half-up port therefore produces a segment that legacy does not. A pure 1-pixel tie: on a 512x512 image '0 0.0400390625 0.5 0.0390625 0.5' gives x1 = round(10.5) = 10 and x2 = round(30.5) = 30, i.e. columns 10..29; half-up gives columns 11..30.
Prediction files that carry a 6th confidence token are skipped line by line, silently and with no class id assigned (:432-434); pinned by tests/unit/core/test_file_manager.py:294-312.

Loaded boxes are masks, not editable rectangles: type is 'Loaded' and vertices is null (:406-407). Every surviving box allocates its own full (h, w) boolean array (:400), so N boxes cost N*h*w booleans.
Duplicate and overlapping lines are all kept as separate segments; overlap pixels are true in both masks and nothing is merged or de-duplicated (tests/unit/core/test_file_manager.py:274-288).

CORRECTION to the card: a same-named non-annotation .txt (a caption file, say) does not 'stop the load chain' — '.txt' is already the LAST entry of _LOAD_CHAIN (:135), so nothing follows it. The real consequence is elsewhere: find_annotation_file (:138-151) reports the image as annotated purely because the .txt exists, so the UI treats it as already labelled (main_window.py:3966, :4226, :4858) while zero segments actually load.

Consequence that makes the failure modes destructive rather than cosmetic: auto-save on navigation defaults to on (file_navigation_manager.py:156-160), and save_single_view_output deletes every annotation sidecar for the image, the source .txt included, whenever the segment list is empty (save_export_manager.py:106-109 -> exporters/__init__.py:208-215). So a whole-file abort, or a file whose lines were all skipped, can erase the user's labels on the next image change. Lines that were individually skipped are likewise lost on any re-save, because the exporter rewrites the same base+'.txt' from the loaded segments only (exporters/yolo_detection.py:44-46).
answer: The open question is whether this card should keep its P0 'copy Python's half-to-even rounding exactly' contract, and the approved decisions settle it: yes. 'Imported annotations must land on exactly the same pixels as legacy' makes the rounding mode, the exclusive x2/y2 bounds and the asymmetric clamp contractual, so the compliance judge's advice to demote to P1 and treat the tie rounding as a non-blocking dual-run check is overruled — and it was based on a false premise anyway, since a tie is not always a 1-pixel shift: on a 1024-wide image a half-up port keeps a box that legacy drops entirely (file_manager.py:446-449 with :397-398). 'Keep legacy per-image class ids and aliases' makes the pre-clamp ordering contractual too, so _build_label_map running over every parsed box at file_manager.py:392 before the clamp and drop at :394-398 must be reproduced, aliases for dropped boxes included (:377, copied into saves at save_worker.py:89 and save_export_manager.py:424). 'A failed or partial load must never present as no annotations' is the one place where the port must diverge from legacy's UX while matching its data: legacy raises out of :446-449, load_existing_mask swallows it at :202-204, and the user sees an empty canvas that auto-save then turns into deletion of the source .txt (file_navigation_manager.py:156-160 -> save_export_manager.py:106-109 -> exporters/__init__.py:208-215), so the port must load the same zero segments but surface a distinguishable load-failure state and must report skipped lines rather than silently presenting a clean empty image. What was wrong in the card: (1) it never mentions the whole-file abort at all — its 'lines without numeric coordinates are skipped' wording is only true for tokens float() rejects, since 'nan', 'inf' and '1e309' pass the try at :437-440 and then raise outside it at :446-449, discarding every valid box in the file; (2) 'Parameters' states the rounding mode twice and still omits the load-bearing details — that image_size is (height, width) (:391), that the halving happens before the multiply (:446-449), that the clamp is asymmetric with no upper bound on x1/y1 and no lower bound on x2/y2 (:395-396), and that Python's float()/int() grammars differ from JavaScript's Number()/parseInt(); (3) the edge case 'still stops the load chain' is wrong because '.txt' is already last in _LOAD_CHAIN (:135) — the real effect is that find_annotation_file (:138-151) marks the image as labelled at main_window.py:3966, :4226 and :4858; (4) 'negative coordinates are clamped to 0' is only half the rule, since the drop test at :397-398 also removes flipped boxes and boxes wholly off-image; (5) the class token's lack of validation and the alias-name-beats-integer resolution order (:362-366) were missing, so '3' is class 3 only when no alias is named '3'. What an implementer must watch for: write a Python-compatible float parser and a half-to-even pyRound before anything else, keep the arithmetic association byte-for-byte as at :446-449, assign class ids before clamping, and make the non-finite case throw and be surfaced instead of quietly yielding an empty segment list.

unresolved: One genuine product decision remains: the legacy text encoding is machine-dependent, because open() at file_manager.py:424 takes the platform locale encoding (cp1252 on the Windows machine this was verified on, UTF-8 on most Linux/macOS installs). 'Exactly the same pixels as legacy' is therefore undefined for any file that is not pure ASCII — the same UTF-8 file with a BOM loads class 0 on Linux and an alias-named garbage class on Windows. The port must pick one: read as UTF-8 and strip a leading BOM (recommended; matches Linux legacy and fixes the BOM class, but diverges from a Windows legacy install for non-ASCII label names), or replicate cp1252 for byte-fidelity with Windows. A second, smaller choice: Python's int() gives arbitrary-precision class ids, so a label like '99999999999999999999' becomes an exact 20-digit class id that JavaScript numbers cannot represent — the owner should confirm whether to use BigInt, cap the id, or treat oversized integer labels as non-numeric and give them a fresh id.
